analysis.analysis:
We evaluate the proposed architecture with accuracy (ACC) and average precision (AP) metrics on each test dataset, following previous works for comparability purposes. For the calculation of accuracy no calibration is conducted, we consider 0.5 as threshold to all methods. We also report the average (AVG) metric values across the test datasets to obtain summary evaluations.

In table 1 and table 2, we present the performance scores (ACC & AP respectively) of our method versus the competing ones. Our 1-class model outperforms all state-of-the-art methods irrespective of training class number. On average, we surpass the state-of-the-art by +9.4% ACC & +4.3% AP with the 1-class model, by +6.8% ACC & +4.4% AP with the 2-class model, and by +10.6% ACC & +4.5% AP with the 4-class model. In terms of ACC, we obtain the best score in 14 out of 20 test datasets, and simultaneously the first and second best performance in 10 of them. In terms of AP, we obtain the best score in 15 out of 20 test datasets, and simultaneously the first and second best performance in 14 of them. The biggest performance gain is on the SAN dataset (+16.9% ACC).

considerations.ethical_risks:
• Risk of false positives: mislabeling authentic images as fake could undermine trust in legitimate sources or individuals.

  • Over-reliance on automated detection without human oversight could lead to unfair consequences in sensitive domains (e.g., journalism, legal evidence).

  • Potential misuse in surveillance or censorship applications under the guise of detecting artificially generated content.
considerations.hardware: • A GPU with at least 4GB of memory
considerations.inputs_outputs:
• Input: RGB Image
  • Output: A negative or positive float that indicates if the image is real or fake respectively

considerations.limitations:
• May have low accuracy on new generative methods without fine-tuning.

  • The reliance on CLIP’s intermediate representations may introduce bias or limit adaptability if CLIP fails to encode certain visual anomalies effectively.

  • Adversarial attacks could reduce robustness.

considerations.use_case:
• Detecting synthetic or fake images generated by various generative models (e.g., GANs, Diffusion models).

  • Enhancing the security and trustworthiness of visual media by identifying manipulated or AI-generated content.

  • Applicable across multiple generative model types and datasets.

eval_set.datasets: The evaluation set can be found in: CNN_synth_testset ( Sheng-Yu Wang et al. ) and diffusion_datasets (Utkarsh Ojha et al.). They contain 20 datasets including generated and real images from: ProGAN, StyleGAN, StyleGAN2, BigGAN, CycleGAN, StarGAN, GauGAN, DeepFake, SITD, SAN, CRN, IMLE, Guided, LDM (3 variants), Glide (3 variants), DALL-E
eval_set.motivation:
The evaluation set was curated to include a wide range of datasets that reflect the diversity of generative image models and manipulation techniques currently available. It spans multiple architectural families, including GANs, diffusion models, and hybrid pipelines, with the aim of testing the generalization and robustness of detection methods across fundamentally different generation strategies. Models such as ProGAN, StyleGAN, and BigGAN represent various stages in the development of GAN architectures, from early iterations to highly realistic, high-resolution generators. Meanwhile, recent diffusion-based models like LDM, Glide, and DALL-E capture the state of the art in iterative denoising approaches, offering a contrast in both generation dynamics and output characteristics.

The dataset selection also reflects a temporal progression in generative model capabilities, enabling evaluation of a system’s resilience to advances in model fidelity and realism. Furthermore, the included datasets vary widely in terms of image content: some focus on photorealistic human faces, others on objects or scenes, and some on artistic or semantically guided transformations, as seen in models like GauGAN and CycleGAN. This variation ensures that the evaluation is not biased toward any particular domain or artifact type.

In addition to synthetic data, the evaluation set includes real images, supporting the assessment of binary real-vs-fake classification tasks. The inclusion of realistic face manipulation techniques, such as DeepFake and StarGAN, introduces additional challenges that reflect real-world concerns around identity falsification and misinformation. Some generative models are represented through multiple variants, enabling fine-grained analysis of how detection performance responds to subtle architectural or configuration differences.

Overall, the motivation behind selecting these datasets is to construct a comprehensive and representative benchmark that can test the limits of detection systems, particularly their ability to generalize to unseen or evolving generative approaches in practical, unconstrained environments.
eval_set.pre_processing:
The data pre-processing procedure used for evaluation follows these steps:

  • Multi-crop generation:
    Each input image is converted into ten fixed 224×224 crops, including the center, four corners, and their horizontal flips. This provides test-time augmentation by capturing multiple spatial perspectives of the same image.

  • Tensor conversion:
    Each crop is transformed from a PIL image into a tensor format suitable for PyTorch-based models.

  • Pixel value scaling:
    All pixel values are divided by 255 to normalize them to the 0,10,1 range, which is a standard preprocessing step for image models.

  • Normalization:
    Crops are normalized using the mean and standard deviation values
    mean = (0.48145466, 0.4578275, 0.40821073) and
    std = (0.26862954, 0.26130258, 0.27577711),
    which correspond to the normalization parameters of CLIP's image encoder. This ensures the input distribution matches the model's training distribution.

  • Batch formation:
    The ten processed crops are stacked into a single tensor batch per image, enabling simultaneous inference over all views during evaluation.
eval_set.update: The datasets included in the evaluation set are of high quality and reflect the current state of generative image synthesis technologies in 2024. Many of the models, such as StyleGAN2, BigGAN, and DALL-E, are widely used in both academic and applied contexts, making them representative of the kinds of synthetic content that may be encountered in real-world deployments. Furthermore, the inclusion of both older and newer models ensures that the evaluation data remains relevant across time, accommodating future shifts in generative model usage. The presence of realistic manipulation techniques and multiple domains (e.g., facial synthesis, style transfer, semantic image generation) enhances the dataset's ability to simulate deployment environments where adversarial or synthetic content varies widely in intent, quality, and origin. As a result, the dataset is well-suited for evaluating systems intended for robust, real-world operation against a diverse and evolving threat landscape.

model.author: CERTH - The Centre for Research & Technology, Hellas
model.name: RINE
model.overview: RINE is a model designed for Synthetic Image Detection (SID) tasks, aimed at detecting fake images generated by various generative models. By leveraging representations from intermediate encoder-blocks of CLIP, RINE focuses on low-level visual information crucial for effective SID. The model utilizes learnable linear mappings and a Trainable Importance Estimator (TIE) module to enhance prediction accuracy. Trained on ProGAN-generated images and evaluated on diverse datasets, including images from GAN, Diffusion, and other generative models, RINE outperforms existing methods by an average of +10.6%. Notably, RINE achieves this superior performance with only 6.3M learnable parameters, trained for just 1 epoch (approximately 8 minutes), surpassing the state-of-the-art by +9.4% even when trained on a single ProGAN object class.

training_set.datasets: Following the training protocol of related work [Ojha. et al. , Wang. et al. , Tan. et al. ], we use for training ProGAN [Karras et al.] generated images and the corresponding real images of the provided dataset. Similarly with previous works [Tan. et al. , Jeong et al.], we consider three settings with ProGAN-generated training data from 1 (horse), 2 (chair, horse) and 4 (car, cat, chair, horse) object classes.
training_set.motivation:
The training of RINE is conducted with batch size 128 and learning rate 1e-3 for only 1 epoch using the Adam optimizer. For each of the 3 training settings (1-class, 2-class, 4-class), we consider a hyperparameter grid to obtain the best performance, namely ξ ∈ {0.1,0.2,0.4,0.8}, q ∈ {1,2,4}, and d′ ∈ {128,256,512,1024}. Additionally, we consider two CLIP variants, namely ViT-B/32 and L/14, for the extraction of representations. The models’ hyperparameters that result in the best performance are illustrated in the bellow table, along with the corresponding number of trainable parameters, and required training duration. For the training images, following the best practice in related work, we apply Gaussian blurring and JPEG compression with probability 0.5, then random cropping to 224×224, and finally random horizontal flip with probability 0.5. The validation and test images are only center-cropped at 224×224. Resizing is omitted both during training and testing as it is known to eliminate synthetic traces. All experiments are conducted using one NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3090 Ti GPU.
